Haven't been on Voat in awhile, but this is still in my feed. Anyways, Im a designer, animator, and developer. The biggest thing I've learned in creating tons of portfolio sites and my own personal sites. Its HARD. Everyone struggles with this, your style changes. Influences change as your work, iterate, develop. Even companies that make their own portfolios struggle with maintaining a concept from start to finish. Theres no easy way, theres no right way. Just spit out your idea, get it down. Get basic concepts, animations, styles down. Finish It. Finish It. Than, take a step back for a bit and decide what you can do to adjust things, polish it, etc. The best thing I've found, is to create a project based on a fake client with fake stylistic goals and fake concepts. Make it tailored to that concept and not what you like, what you find is cool to do. This takes a lot of your personal ideas and stylistic choices away from what your trying to create. I had this coworker who got a prime developer position with no real work to show by creating fake sites for fake clients that was really well done, design and code wise. They never made it further than his portfolio, but it showed that he could adapt to different style and keep his code clean.

First, I should point out that I have no affiliation with any gray market software site or vendor.

For those not clear on what the software gray market is, it's kind of like e-bay for software keys. Some people have keys, other people have money. A gray market site facilitates the transaction in a very familiar e-commerce setting.

The reason why it's called a gray market is because the buyers and sellers aren't, strictly speaking, breaking any laws. It's unconventional and potentially risky but not illegal.

Last year, there was a scandal involving the sale of registration keys for Ubisoft games through a gray market site. As it turns out, those keys were purchased with credit card data stolen when EA's customer data was hacked (how's that for two birds with one stone?). When Ubisoft found out which keys were affected, they deactivated them, leaving customers who paid good money on the gray market site irate that their "legitimate" keys were taken from them. Of course, they weren't legitimate at the source which meant they weren't legit to sell and thus not legit to activate a copy of the game, but we all know how consumers are when they get burned. "Fuck anyone else, just not me." Ubisoft eventually relented, but not before one of the gray market sites issued refunds to its customers in the range of $170,000.

That little scandal taught us something important. When doing business with a go-between like e-bay, or amazon, or a gray market software site, there's a chance you might get burned. Investigate your options and what avenues are available to protect yourself before making a purchase and if you're not comfortable with the risk, don't take the risk.

Where do these heavily discounted keys come from? Well, you know when Steam has sales with games that normally retail for $50-60 (or more) and end up 80% off for a while? If you buy a bunch of gift keys, wait for the sale to end, and then sell those gift keys at 50% off retail, you make a few bucks when the dust settles. That's just one example. Other examples that might be less scrupulous (but functionally impossible to track) might be things like, "Hey, I work for and we just got a shitload of Steam codes for the new Hitman game to give away with high end AMD cards...nobody will notice if a few of these are redirected."

"Don't ask, don't tell," as they say. The site that hosts the transaction only knows if the keys the vendor sells actually work. The vendor's reputation is based on making sure the customer gets a working key. Where that key comes from, on the other hand, is impossible to verify. So the guy who was all jazzed to be getting a code for Rise of the Tomb Raider when he picks up his new GTX 970 hybrid only to be told the retailer is out of codes, so sorry...he kinda maybe got screwed by Bob the grey market trader.

From a developer perspective, all fraud and overtly illegal stuff aside, the benefit they get out of running sales can easily be undermined by gray market vendors buying up keys to sell and then maintaining a retail environment away from the developer's own channels that beats the developers' regular price. The brand loyalty and consumer interest that was supposed to have been sparked by the sale is instead being used to run someone else' business.

I've only made one purchase through the gray market and it wasn't even for a game. Through a chance chain of events I found myself directed to a site that offered an OEM key for Windows 10 Pro for $30 (my local vendor lists it at $220 regular price). I did my "due diligence" and was satisfied that everything was on the up-and-up so I went for it, but I can't register the code yet because my CPU is backordered and my GPU isn't available for sale yet :P Consequently, I can't say if I got what I paid for, but it seemed an interesting topic.

This is one of the articles I read when doing my homework prior to making a purchase:

http://www.polygon.com/2015/2/9/8006693/the-truth-behind-those-mysteriously-cheap-gray-market-game-codes

Do you buy from gray market vendors? If you have, has your experience been good? Are you opposed to this segment of the industry? Would you prefer that vendors like Steam, EA, etc. set up their systems so that no key actually exists and thus make it impossible for gray market vendors who rely on these channels to obtain heavily discounted keys?
Gray market games: Good for the consumers? Bad for the devs? Bad for consumers? Who cares about devs?

Another example of gray market goods: Accounts.

League of Legends uses a grind to gate access to ranked play. People will buy accounts to play on ranked, either to practice new strategies without risking their main ranking or sometimes just to pubstomp. Not only is this money that Riot is not capturing but it also severely hurts the nature of the game as each of these accounts distorts matchmaking for players matched with these players.

That wouldn't be a gray market good. That would be a black market good. You have to agree to a ToS to play on an account and make it attractive for sale, and that ToS forbids you from transferring that account to a third party. You have to violate a legally binding agreement to sell an account. A product key is a product key, and if there are circumstances where a key is issued with acceptance of particular terms, neither the transaction site nor the buyer can know that the seller is violating those terms. More "don't ask, don't tell" stuff. But if you see an account for an MMORPG or a MOBA for sale, you know straight away that that's in contravention of a binding agreement. There's no doubt about it. Ergo, black vs. gray.

It depends on what you think of as "grey market" sites. I buy from cdkeys.com, greenmangaming, Nuuvem, etc. I already have far too many games on my backlog to justify paying full price, so if I don't find it at a low enough price on those sites, I simply wait for a sale.

No. I only buy from known reputable vendors such as Steam, GoG, humble bundle, etc. I also will pay full price for a game if I feel it's good rather than waiting for sales. I understand others may have budget constraints and I'm ok with that, but personally I think developers should be well compensated for their work when the result is good.

We need to break out of this mentality that we are owed games and start understanding that everything is driven by the money. Showing devs we'll pay fair market prices for games we like is good incentive to keep making games we like.
